Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette: Mr. Nguyen is a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has been struggling with profound emotional distress following the tragic loss of his younger brother in a maritime accident six months ago. Mr. Nguyen's brother was a fellow fisherman, and they often worked together out at sea. The day of the accident, their boat capsized during a sudden storm. Despite his efforts to save his brother, Mr. Nguyen watched helplessly as his sibling was swept away by the waves. Since that fateful day, Mr. Nguyen has been plagued by strong physical reactions whenever something reminds him of the traumatic event. Simple sounds like the roar of the sea or the creaking of wooden boats trigger immediate panic and a pounding heart. He also experiences intense negative emotions such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame, making it difficult for him to engage in his daily activities. Mr. Nguyen's mistrust in people has grown significantly since the accident. He now believes that nobody can be trusted, and this belief further exacerbates his distress. The thought of going out to sea again evokes a deep sense of dread and fear, reinforcing his negative appraisals that he is alone and vulnerable. This mistrust also extends to his interactions with other fishermen in his community; he feels increasingly isolated and finds it hard to form close connections. His emotional numbness adds another layer to his suffering. Mr. Nguyen often describes feeling "dead inside," unable to connect emotionally with others, including his wife. The survival guilt he carries weighs heavily on him—he frequently wonders why he survived when his brother did not. This guilt is a constant source of pain and contributes to the cycle of negative thoughts that make it difficult for him to find any peace or joy in life. Mr. Nguyen's physical reactions are often triggered by memories of the accident, leading to heightened anxiety and emotional distress. The fear of another maritime tragedy or even minor incidents at sea can send him into a state of panic, further reinforcing his negative appraisals that he cannot trust anyone or anything around him. This cycle has made it increasingly difficult for Mr. Nguyen to continue working as a fisherman, impacting both his livelihood and his sense of purpose. Despite these challenges, what finally brought Mr. Nguyen to seek help was the realization that his emotional numbness and mistrust were affecting his relationship with his wife. She had noticed changes in him but couldn't understand why he was withdrawing emotionally. He felt deeply ashamed for not being able to provide for their family and for failing to connect with her on a deeper level. Mr. Nguyen is most afraid of continuing this cycle of guilt, mistrust, and emotional numbness without finding any relief or support. He hopes that through therapy, he can regain a sense of trust in others, find peace with his survivor's guilt, and reconnect with the life he once knew before the accident.
